articles.title: 'Discontent answered with bullets': MEA slams Pakistan over PoK crackdown
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday slammed Pakistan for its ongoing crackdown on protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, calling .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday slammed Pakistan for its ongoing crackdown on protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, calling upon the international community to hold the country accountable for the "gross violation of human rights."During the bi-weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that public discontent in PoK was answered with bullets and blackouts by authorities in Pakistan."We would like to highlight the human rights violations being committed in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and other parts of the country. We call upon the international community to hold Pakistan accountable for its misdeeds, abuses and gross violations of human rights, including against its own people," Jaiswal said."Over the last several months, we have seen large-scale protests in PoK, including during and before the elections. Public discontent was answered with bullets, blackouts, repression and oppression. More than 90 people have been killed and many more injured. This has made news across the world," he added.Also Read | 'Arunachal is integral part of India, nothing can change this': MEA on China's fresh 'objections'The remarks came as at least 90 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July.The banned Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) has been staging protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) since June over the contentious 12 refugee seats. It has alleged that Pakistan's establishment manipulates these seats to install a prime minister of its choice to lead the so-called PoK government.Meanwhile, the third phase of elections in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) was held on Monday in four constituencies, amid violence and allegations of rigging. Polling started in Poonch Division’s Bagh and Haveli districts at 8 am, while elections in seven constituencies have been indefinitely postponed.Clashes between Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) workers were reported in some areas as the region's election commission classified most of the 803 polling stations as "sensitive or highly sensitive".After the first and second phases of polling, which were marred by violent protests and were held on July 27 and August 2, respectively, voting was scheduled for Monday in 11 constituencies of the Poonch Division in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. There are 53 seats in the so-called PoK Legislative Assembly - 45 are directly elected, while eight are reserved for women, technocrats and clerics.The second phase of polling on August 2 was marred by violence and allegations of rigging. One person was killed and several others were injured.Also read | British national killed in PoK clashes; another held for over 2 months, says reportThe phase also included voting for the 12 refugee seats, which are at the centre of the ongoing controversy.Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) swept the second phase, winning 16 seats, while Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) secured the remaining five. In the first phase on July 27, PML-N won nine of the 13 seats, while PPP won four. With the first two phases combined, PML-N has already secured 24 seats.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Bangladesh sets tough riders for PM Tarique Rahman's visit to India
articles.summary: South Asia News: DHAKA/DELHI: Amid mounting domestic pressure from hardliners and opposition Jamaat-e-Islami ally NCP, PM Tarique Rahman's govt Sunday attached tough c.
articles.body: DHAKA/DELHI: Amid mounting domestic pressure from hardliners and opposition Jamaat-e-Islami ally NCP, PM Tarique Rahman's govt Sunday attached tough conditions for New Delhi prior to his possible bilateral visit to India at PM Modi's invitation - "act expeditiously on extradition of Sheikh Hasina and other criminal fugitives, and help create a 'propitious environment' for him to make the visit".The development is being seen by many in diplomatic circles as "surrendering" to opposition forces' call to put forward some "tough conditions" that are apparently impossible for the Indian side to accommodate immediately.According to Indian govt sources, the invitation to Tarique for both Brics and the bilateral visit stands and it's for Dhaka to decide about the timing of the visit.However, the latest statement has effectively ruled out a bilateral visit this week that was under discussion.Asked about the issue related to former Bangladesh PM Hasina, sources in Delhi recalled remarks by governing BNP functionaries earlier that it will not come in the way of Dhaka's efforts to pursue broader relations with India, particularly on issues it considers crucial like trade, energy and water-sharing.On Hasina's extradition request, official sources in Dhaka reiterated it is being examined by Indian authorities in accordance with applicable laws and established legal procedures.Reading out a statement, ministry of foreign affairs spokesperson AKM Shahidul Karim said, "Officials of Bangladesh and India have been in touch...on the possibility of a bilateral visit by PM to India. We are of the view that a propitious environment needs to be created for the visit.""This process was vitiated by the open press interaction in New Delhi on Aug 5 by Sheikh Hasina, who has been convicted by International Crimes Tribunal for committing crimes against humanity," he said, "We have made our position clear on this matter.""...Bangladesh requested Indian authorities to expeditiously act on its request to extradite Sheikh Hasina and to hand over to Bangladesh the accused killers of Shaheed Sharif Osman Hadi in compliance with their bilateral extradition treaty. We are awaiting their response," he said."Govt is under pressure on a number of domestic issues, including energy crisis while Hasina's extradition issue remains unresolved...the relations may even get stalled until Dec...." a political source said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Cash, gold bars by drone: China's PLA stages 'wartime' Taiwan drill
articles.summary: China News: China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has used a multi-rotor drone to deliver cases containing gold bars, New Taiwan dollars and US currency during a.
articles.body: China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has used a multi-rotor drone to deliver cases containing gold bars, New Taiwan dollars and US currency during a “wartime financial support” exercise, in a drill that appeared to simulate the logistical demands of a potential operation against Taiwan.The exercise was conducted by the PLA Eastern Theatre Command, according to a state media report published last week by national newspaper Defence Times. The report, which has since been deleted, showed drones dropping camouflage-covered cases at designated locations before soldiers retrieved and opened them.Photographs released with the report showed troops in tactical camouflage uniforms counting bundles of NT$1,000 notes and US$100 bills alongside gold bars. One of the cases bore the PLA emblem and was marked “Settlement Office No 4, Nanjing Centralised Funds Receipt and Payment Management Centre”.The report did not specify when or where the drill took place, and it was unclear whether the cash and gold displayed during the exercise were genuine.The inclusion of New Taiwan dollars alongside US dollars and gold was particularly notable. While US currency and gold are widely accepted forms of payment, the presence of Taiwan’s currency suggests the PLA may be preparing for circumstances in which troops operating on the island could need to make payments to local residents or businesses.In a wartime scenario, frontline units could require physical currency to purchase supplies and services, obtain intelligence, compensate civilians for damage or cover other expenses when conventional banking networks and electronic payment systems are unavailable or disrupted.The drone-based delivery system also points to an effort to integrate financial logistics into battlefield operations. Using unmanned aircraft could allow cash and other valuables to be moved to forward positions without exposing personnel to the risks involved in transporting them by road or other conventional means.The exercise comes against the backdrop of the PLA's continued preparations for potential military contingencies involving Taiwan. The Eastern Theatre Command is responsible for military operations in the direction of the Taiwan Strait and regularly conducts exercises involving forces from the army, navy, air force and rocket force.The deleted report has nevertheless drawn attention online, particularly over the unusual combination of battlefield logistics, foreign currency and gold. The display of New Taiwan dollars has added to speculation that the exercise was designed with a Taiwan contingency in mind, although the available report does not explicitly state that the drill simulated an invasion or occupation of the island.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iran claims control, ships choose Omani route: What’s changing in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Middle East News: The battle for control of the Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a key focus of the Iran war, with both Iran and the United States claiming the upper han.
articles.body: The battle for control of the Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a key focus of the Iran war, with both Iran and the United States claiming the upper hand in recent months. The competing claims have created uncertainty over the extent of control exercised by either side over the critical waterway.However, shipping data indicates that the United States is gaining ground as its navy patrols the strait, while Iran appears to be losing control over parts of the waterway.More than 80% of vessel that have transited through the Strait of Hormuz over the past two weeks have used the Omani route, a UN-authorised shipping channel opposed by Iran, according to Kpler, which tracks vessels using transponders and satellite data cited by CNN.Shipping traffic slows amid uncertaintyShipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed on Tuesday, with preliminary data showing most shipowners continued to avoid the key waterway amid a lack of clear signals on its reopening, Reuters reported.Iran, which has declared the Strait of Hormuz under its control, has attacked dozens of ships attempting to transit the waterway along Oman’s northern coast.Despite the risks, most vessels have recently continued to cross the strait, disregarding Iran’s demands and relying on protection from US naval forces.The expiration of the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding this week has, in theory, allowed Iran to resume charging tolls on vessels using the Strait of Hormuz. However, Kpler data suggests that Iran has not been able to do so.The current traffic pattern marks a sharp contrast with a month ago, when Kpler recorded virtually no shipping activity along the Omani route. The steep decline in traffic along Iran’s preferred route has also prevented Tehran from collecting tolls on vessels passing through the strait, as it did in the spring.Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have chartered Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), the largest oil tankers, to transport crude out of the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz. The oil is then transferred to customers’ tankers outside the danger zone in the Gulf of Oman, according to Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.To avoid Iranian attacks, the tankers have switched off their transponders, sometimes for weeks at a time. Such “dark traffic” can evade some tracking services, including Kpler, although some vessels can still be detected through satellite data.The United States, however, has deployed significant military forces in the waterway and has reported substantially higher oil-shipping volumes than earlier estimates from traditional tracking services.US claims control as Oman-Iran talks continueUS President Donald Trump said Monday that the United States had “total control over the strait”, a claim he has repeatedly made during the conflict. However, continued Iranian attacks and oil flows remaining well below pre-war levels suggest that the US does not have full control of the Strait of Hormuz.At the same time, if tankers are moving as much oil through the strait as the United States claims, Iran’s ability to deter shipping and maintain control of the waterway has weakened compared with a month or two ago.Meanwhile, Oman and Iran are holding talks to restore freedom of navigation through the strait without US involvement. The discussions could affect oil traffic and control of the strategic waterway, though their impact remains unclear.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: European wild boars escaped a North Carolina hunting ranch in 1912; a century later the Smokies still removes hundreds each year to limit their damage
articles.summary: Europe News: A shipment of European wild boars brought to a North Carolina hunting estate more than a century ago continues to cause serious ecological problems in.
articles.body: A shipment of European wild boars brought to a North Carolina hunting estate more than a century ago continues to cause serious ecological problems inside Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Park officials remove about 275 wild hogs every year to limit damage to fragile mountain habitats, according to data from the National Park Service’s species guide for the park. The animals trace their roots to 1912, when 13 wild boars arrived at a private 1,600 acre game preserve on Hooper Bald in Graham County, North Carolina. The preserve was created by George Gordon Moore, an adviser to English investors who owned local timber lands. The imported boars were kept alongside buffalo, elk, bears and thousands of game birds inside a fenced enclosure. However, the animals soon proved difficult to contain. Historical records from the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission say that during a hunt with dogs about eight to 10 years after their arrival, the frightened boars jumped over low sections of the rail fence and escaped into the surrounding mountain forests. By the late 1940s, the roaming animals had reached the area that became part of Great Smoky Mountains National Park. As they spread, they bred with feral domestic pigs left behind by former mountain homesteaders, producing a tough hybrid hog. The animals kept traits of their European ancestors, including long legs, coarse black coats, dark tusks and aggressive feeding habits.Damage to high country ecosystemsThe ecological damage became clear to park managers in the late 1950s. In a historical account published by the National Archives Prologue blog, supervisory archivist Patrick Connelly wrote that park rangers in the summer of 1959 found widespread root damage across the scenic high altitude balds. These grassy mountain tops, covered with native shrubs and rare flowering plants such as pink shell azaleas, were highly vulnerable to soil erosion. Park officials soon discovered that the non-native boars were moving to higher elevations to dig for grubs, earthworms and plant roots. Cattle grazing before the national park was created had helped produce large grub populations, making the balds major feeding areas for the hogs. Unlike native mammals, wild hogs use their strong snouts to dig through the topsoil. This rooting behavior destroys native wildflowers, damages young trees and changes the structure of the soil. It also encourages invasive weeds while reducing food sources such as acorns and hickory nuts for native animals including black bears and white-tailed deer. In response to the damage, park authorities began a two-part control programme in 1959. Working with game management officials from Tennessee, rangers used live traps and hired hunters to shoot free-roaming boars during weekly patrols. Officials also treated pastures to reduce grub populations.Ongoing management and barriers to eradicationDespite decades of control efforts, completely removing wild hogs remains almost impossible because of the dense forests, steep mountain slopes and high reproductive rate of the animals. Female hogs can produce two litters a year, with as many as six piglets per litter. This allows populations to recover quickly when control efforts slow down. Today, the National Park Service uses live trapping, targeted shooting and protective fencing to protect the most sensitive plant communities. Captured animals are removed from the park, while temporary fences are placed around rare plant areas to stop hogs from reaching and damaging them. The agency works with wildlife departments in North Carolina and Tennessee, along with federal partners, to maintain control efforts. Wild hogs also create other risks. They can spread diseases such as pseudorabies and swine brucellosis to livestock in nearby farming communities. They also pollute streams and springs by rolling in mud to cool themselves during summer, increasing water turbidity and damaging small aquatic habitats. More than 110 years after escaping from a private hunting enclosure in western North Carolina, descendants of those European wild boars remain one of the South’s toughest wildlife management challenges.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trouble brewing for Zelenskyy? Ex-defence minister calls for wartime polls
articles.summary: Europe News: Ukraine’s recently dismissed former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for presidential elections to be held despite the ongoing war with Ru.
articles.body: Ukraine’s recently dismissed former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for presidential elections to be held despite the ongoing war with Russia, delivering one of the most direct political challenges to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy since the full-scale invasion began in 2022.In a nine-minute video address posted online, Fedorov argued that Ukraine must restore a “full democratic process” even while fighting Russia. “Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state,” the 35-year-old said. Although he did not name Zelenskyy, his remarks amounted to a sharp criticism of the way the country is being governed, including concerns over corruption, appointments and a lack of accountability.Fedorov’s intervention comes weeks after Zelenskyy abruptly removed him as defence minister, only six months after his appointment. His dismissal triggered rare wartime protests in Kyiv and has fuelled speculation about growing tensions within Ukraine’s political establishment. Zelenskyy has not publicly responded to the call for elections.Why Fedorov’s election call mattersUkraine has been under martial law since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, and elections are suspended under the country’s legal framework. Zelenskyy’s five-year presidential term formally expired in May 2024, but the continuation of martial law has prevented a vote from taking place.Fedorov argued that the prolonged war should not permanently put democratic politics on hold. “We must find a legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to restore a full democratic process even amid a prolonged war,” he said.The appeal could prove politically significant because Fedorov is not an outsider. A former digital minister and one of the prominent young reformers in Zelenskyy’s team, he played a key role in Ukraine’s wartime adoption of drone technology and other innovations. His sudden removal, reportedly amid tensions with military leadership, had already exposed divisions within the government.Recent polling cited in the material suggests Fedorov could emerge as a serious contender in a future presidential race. He was placed behind Zelenskyy and former armed forces chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi in a first-round scenario, but polling indicated that both Fedorov and Zaluzhnyi could defeat Zelenskyy in a run-off.Why a wartime election would be extremely difficultHolding an election while the war continues would present enormous logistical and security challenges. Russian missile and drone attacks regularly target Ukrainian cities, while fighting stretches across a front line of more than 1,200km.Millions of Ukrainians have also been displaced. More than 4 million are living under temporary protection in the European Union, while millions more are internally displaced. Around 1 million people are serving in Ukraine’s defence forces, including personnel deployed near the frontline.The situation is further complicated by Russian occupation of roughly a fifth of Ukraine. Ensuring voting rights for people in occupied areas, protecting polling stations and preventing Russian interference would all require new legal and security arrangements.A Ukrainian political analyst cited in the material said there was a deep-rooted view that elections were necessary, but only after the “hot phase” of the war ended. Even Fedorov’s supporters face the question of how a genuinely free and safe vote could be organised while Russian attacks continue.Zelenskyy faces a wider political testFedorov’s intervention comes as Zelenskyy faces renewed scrutiny over corruption and the functioning of his administration. Ukraine’s anti-corruption agencies have launched a probe involving current and former officials, including an unnamed official in the presidential office. Zelenskyy subsequently dismissed deputy presidential office head Iryna Mudra, although investigators have not named her as a suspect.The developments add to political pressure on a president whose popularity, while still significant, has fallen from its extraordinary wartime levels. The latest controversy also follows previous public anger over government attempts to curb the powers of anti-corruption agencies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Valkyrae’s AI controversy grows as streamer reveals the artist behind her disputed YouTube thumbnail
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Rachell “Valkyrae” Hofstetter has addressed a growing debate over the artwork used for her YouTube livestreams after viewers accused her latest thumbn.
articles.body: Rachell “Valkyrae” Hofstetter has addressed a growing debate over the artwork used for her YouTube livestreams after viewers accused her latest thumbnail of being AI-generated. The streamer defended her longtime thumbnail artist, Anko, while admitting she understands why some people reached that conclusion. Her comments also highlight a wider concern for digital artists as AI-generated content continues to reshape how audiences view online artwork.Valkyrae addresses AI allegations over YouTube thumbnailThe controversy began after Anko, Valkyrae’s thumbnail artist, shared the creative process behind artwork for her Uncharted playthrough. The thumbnail initially received attention from viewers, but some quickly questioned whether artificial intelligence had been used to create it.That reaction eventually reached Valkyrae, who explained that Anko creates all of her YouTube livestream thumbnails and regularly shares his process online. She also pointed out the irony of the situation, saying that even those behind-the-scenes videos have not stopped people from making AI accusations.Valkyrae said:"Okay. We have to talk about this thumbnail debacle. I don't know what to do about this thumbnail debacle. So, as most of you know, every single one of my YouTube livestream thumbnails is made by the same artist. His name is Anko, and he makes all of them. He even posts on Twitter the art process of making them, but it still never beats the AI allegations. And the most recent thumbnail, he makes new thumbnails when I start a new game series, so, obviously, there is a new thumbnail for the Uncharted era. And people were saying, 'Oh, it's AI slop,' in the pre-chat."The streamer then offered a more nuanced response. Rather than dismissing viewers who suspected AI, she said she understood where their reaction came from. At the same time, she wanted to make clear that the artwork was not created using AI.Valkyrae added:"'Just ignore them.' Well, no. Okay? I don't blame people for thinking it's AI because AI is using people's art, like Anko's, to take over. But I would like to clear it up because there were a few people that were saying, 'Oh! When I saw the thumb, I also thought it was AI.' So now I am wondering how many people are out there that would watch the stream, but didn't because of the AI-looking thumbnail! But it's not AI."Valkyrae defends thumbnail artist AnkoThe discussion also became personal for Valkyrae because she said she felt bad for Anko. The thumbnail was later updated, with the artist adding his signature, giving viewers another indication of who created the work.Valkyrae explained that the situation made her think about the broader impact AI tools could have on working artists. For creators who depend on commissioned digital artwork, being mistaken for AI-generated work can create a difficult problem. The visual style that once helped an artist stand out can now cause audiences to question whether a human created it at all.She said:"I don't know, dude. I don't know what to do about it. I feel bad for him, though, because... and then, it, like, reminded me. I was like, 'Man, I just shouldn't do art thumbnails.' But then, the whole AI thing is doing what it does - making artists lose their jobs! Isn't that crazy?!"The controversy has now become more than a discussion about one YouTube thumbnail. Valkyrae’s response reflects a growing tension between AI-generated imagery and human-made digital art, particularly on social media where polished artwork can be judged within seconds.For Valkyrae, however, the message is straightforward: the Uncharted thumbnail was made by Anko, not AI. The debate instead shows how difficult it has become for artists to prove the human work behind their creations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Overnight Russian missile strikes leave 6 dead, 33 wounded across Kyiv
articles.summary: Europe News: At least six people were killed and 33 wounded in Kyiv after Russia launched an overnight missile barrage that damaged residential buildings and publi.
articles.body: At least six people were killed and 33 wounded in Kyiv after Russia launched an overnight missile barrage that damaged residential buildings and public facilities as explosions continued across the capital into Thursday morning.In the Solomianskyi district, the upper two floors of a nine-storey residential building were destroyed, while fires broke out on other floors. People were also trapped inside two residential buildings and a school shelter.The attack struck 12 locations across the Darnytskyi, Sviatoshynskyi and Solomianskyi districts, including a medical facility and an educational institution. Emergency workers rescued people from beneath the debris as the air raid alert continued into the early morning, according to the Associated Press (AP).Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the overnight assault combined ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones, killing 12 people in Kyiv and one more in the surrounding region, while leaving around 40 others injured. He said Ukraine still lacked sufficient anti-ballistic defences and warned that Patriot interceptors remained urgently needed.Russia has stepped up ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv in an effort to strain Ukraine's air-defence stocks. The capital has only a limited number of systems capable of countering such threats.Interceptor missiles for Ukraine's US-made Patriot systems are also in persistently short supply, adding to the pressure on Kyiv's ability to defend against ballistic attacks.US President Donald Trump had previously authorised Ukraine to obtain licences to produce Patriot air-defence systems before reversing the decision.Ukraine has also expanded its long-range strikes deep inside Russia, hitting arms depots, military installations and other strategic targets as part of an effort to erode Moscow's capacity to continue attacks on Ukrainian cities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1927, a woman bought an English island for £125,000 to create a refuge for animals; she lived reclusively there for 34 years
articles.summary: UK News: Discover how Mary Bonham-Christie's purchase of Brownsea Island turned it into a secluded sanctuary for wildlife over 34 years, preserving nature amidst changing times.
articles.body: In 1927, Mary Bonham-Christie paid £125,000 for Brownsea Island in Dorset and began turning the private estate into a refuge where wildlife could flourish away from the bustle of human society. At 62, she withdrew from the social life associated with the island, moved into the Agent’s House on the quay and increasingly kept people away from her property. For the next 34 years, until she died in 1961, she lived reclusively on Brownsea while allowing much of the island’s landscape to become wilder.Her approach was a striking departure from the way Brownsea had been managed earlier in the century. According to the Dorset Natural History and Archaeological Society Proceedings, Charles and Florence van Raalte bought the island in 1901. They turned it into a centre of Edwardian social life, hosting wealthy and titled guests for parties, holidays and shooting weekends. The estate employed servants, farm workers, gamekeepers, builders and boatmen, and the island supported a busy community during their ownership. Bonham-Christie took the same island in the opposite direction. Instead of filling it with guests and activity, she increasingly shut it off, creating the secluded environment that would define her 34-year ownership.From country estate to wildlife refugeBonham-Christie’s priorities were markedly different from those of the previous owners. She had a strong dislike of activities that involved killing animals and stopped shooting and fishing on the island. Dairy farming was abandoned, orchards were left unattended, and the daffodil fields that had once supplied the Covent Garden flower market were no longer cultivated. Farm animals were allowed to roam rather than being kept within the tightly managed agricultural system that had operated before her arrival.The transformation also changed life for the people who worked on the estate. Many lost their jobs and returned to the mainland as Bonham-Christie became increasingly protective of her privacy and restricted access to the island. Historic England describes her as Brownsea’s last private occupier and notes that the resident population was relocated to the mainland during her ownership. As regular estate management declined, fields, gardens and orchards were gradually left less intensively managed. Woodland and heathland expanded, giving wildlife a more varied landscape in which to survive. Brownsea was not completely cut off from human activity, however. During the Second World War, refugees were housed on the island and military operations caused further disturbance. Even so, the long-term decline in farming and estate activity changed Brownsea’s character, leaving wildlife with more space and less day-to-day human interference.An isolated refuge during a changing centuryThe Second World War brought another unexpected role for the island. Brownsea briefly sheltered exhausted Dutch and Belgian refugees in 1940. The following year, a night decoy was established on its western side, using flares to make German bombers believe they were approaching the nearby towns of Poole and Bournemouth. The decoy site succeeded, but the operation also damaged the abandoned settlement of Maryland. Even during these years of upheaval, however, Brownsea's relative isolation continued to shape what happened to its landscape and wildlife.That isolation later became particularly important for the island's red squirrels. According to Ecology and Evolution, red squirrels in southern England are now restricted to Brownsea Island, Furzey Island and the Isle of Wight, with genetic analysis identifying private haplotypes that may represent distinct genetic lineages important for conservation. Biodiversity and Conservation likewise reports that these island populations remain largely isolated from competition with grey squirrels, although their small size and geographic isolation leave them vulnerable.What happened after the recluse died?Mary Bonham-Christie died in 1961, aged 96, bringing 34 years of private ownership to an end. Her death left Brownsea facing an uncertain future. The island was at risk of development, with proposals reportedly including hundreds of houses. Local conservationists, led by Helen Brotherton, organised a campaign to protect it from being transformed into a residential estate.Their efforts eventually opened the island to a new chapter. The woman who had spent decades keeping people away was gone, but the landscape she had protected through her isolation was still there. Conservationists and later owners worked to preserve Brownsea rather than turn it into the development that had once been proposed. Today, Brownsea retains traces of its earlier estate history, while its woodlands, heathlands and wildlife have become an important part of the island’s landscape.The island’s next chapter also brought a change in how Brownsea was valued. What had once been treated largely as a private estate came to be recognised for its ecological importance, particularly its mix of woodland, heath and wetland habitats. Over time, conservation management shifted the focus from keeping people out to protecting the island’s wildlife while allowing carefully managed public access.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US's secret Hormuz corridor: How America kept ships and oil moving despite Iran's closure
articles.summary: Middle East News: The US military secretly helped commercial tankers navigate the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks despite Iran's closure of the strategic waterway. The.
articles.body: The US military secretly helped commercial tankers navigate the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks despite Iran's closure of the strategic waterway. The operation allowed millions of barrels of oil to reach global markets each day despite the ongoing war with Iran, according to an Axios report citing two US officials familiar with the operation.As per the report, the operation allowed 15–20 tankers to move through a southern channel of the strait each night under US military guidance. This carried close to 10 million barrels of oil a day, roughly half the volume that passed through the waterway before the war.The previously unreported operation has provided a crucial channel for keeping oil exports moving at a time when the conflict has severely disrupted one of the world's most important energy routes. The flow has helped ease pressure on global oil supplies after the war sent crude prices sharply higher.How the US operation worksThe US effort involves more than escorting tankers already carrying oil out of the Gulf. American forces are also helping empty tankers travel from the Arabian Sea through the Strait of Hormuz into Gulf ports, where they load oil before making the return journey.The ships are organised into scheduled inbound and outbound convoys each night. The vessels then use the southern lane of the strait based on instructions from the US military."We have been controlling the southern lane of the Strait of Hormuz for two months now. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps can be a nuisance, but they don't control the strait. We do," one of the US officials, who has direct knowledge of the matter, told Axios.The task force coordinating the operation is based at the Army headquarters in Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and works with Gulf partners to compile daily lists of tankers moving through the strait.US Air Force fighter jets are also providing protection against Iranian drones and cruise missiles as the vessels make the crossing.Iran's ability to monitor traffic weakenedAccording to the US officials, the operation became possible after a two-week US Central Command campaign weakened Iran's radar and maritime surveillance capabilities.Iran now has limited visibility over traffic moving through the southern channel, relying on a small number of restored radar systems and "spotters" operating from IRGC fast boats, the officials said.With its surveillance capabilities degraded, Iran has been launching drones and cruise missiles towards areas where it believes commercial ships may be travelling.Some vessels have been struck during Iranian attacks, but US forces have intercepted others. Earlier this week, US forces shot down eight Iranian drones and two cruise missiles, one of the officials said.Oil exports approach 10 million barrels a dayThe operation has kept oil flowing despite the broader conflict. US officials said 15–20 tankers have been transiting the strait each night over the past two weeks, with average daily exports now approaching 10 million barrels.On some days, as many as 15 million to 20 million barrels of oil moved out of the Gulf. More than 20 ships were scheduled to cross the southern lane on one night this week, potentially carrying about 15 million barrels of oil.The volumes remain below pre-war levels, but US officials say the continuing shipments are making a noticeable difference to global energy supplies."There is a tremendous amount of oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz," President Trump told Axios on Wednesday.Trump also said the US was not currently negotiating with Iran, saying, "They are wasting time. It's a waste of time to negotiate with them," he said."The Iranians still have some fight left, but overall they are a shell of themselves," Trump said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2016, Turkey sank a retired Airbus A300 into the Aegean Sea to create an artificial reef for marine life
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In June 2016, authorities in Turkey carried out an unusual experiment off the Aegean coast near the resort town of Kuşadası, deliberately sinking a re.
articles.body: In June 2016, authorities in Turkey carried out an unusual experiment off the Aegean coast near the resort town of Kuşadası, deliberately sinking a retired Airbus A300 passenger jet to create an artificial reef. The aircraft, purchased by the Aydın provincial government for around 270,000 Turkish lira, or roughly $93,000 at the time, was lowered into the sea to a depth of about 75 feet, where officials hoped it would eventually become a habitat for marine life while also creating a new attraction for divers. Measuring about 177 feet long with a wingspan of roughly 144 feet, the aircraft was among the largest planes ever deliberately sunk for the purpose of creating an artificial reef. Authorities also hoped the unusual underwater attraction would help draw as many as 250,000 visitors annually to the region, while directing some diving activity away from natural reefs that had come under pressure from tourism. This creative approach to repurposing decommissioned aircraft demonstrates how unconventional environmental solutions can simultaneously benefit local economies and marine ecosystems in unexpected ways.Why Turkey chose to sink an Airbus A300 in the Aegean SeaThe Airbus project was part of a broader effort by Turkish authorities to expand Kuşadası's diving tourism and create new underwater attractions. Several smaller aircraft had already been deliberately submerged elsewhere along Turkey's coastline, but the A300 represented a much more ambitious undertaking. The aircraft was transported to its final location and supported using inflatable equipment before being carefully lowered into the water. Divers were involved in guiding the enormous fuselage toward the seabed as water entered the aircraft, eventually bringing it to rest roughly 75 feet beneath the surface. The entire sinking operation took approximately two and a half hours, with boats gathering around the area to watch the unusual spectacle. Contemporary reporting by the Washington Post described the project as an attempt to attract both fish and tourists, combining an eye-catching diving attraction with an artificial habitat intended to encourage marine life to colonise the wreck.What officials hoped the artificial reef would achieveLocal officials saw the aircraft as more than an unusual underwater landmark. Aydın mayor Özlem Çerçioğlu attended the sinking and said the project was intended to help establish Kuşadası as an important destination for diving tourism while contributing to the protection of underwater ecosystems. The strategy was to provide divers with a new attraction that could absorb some of the pressure placed on natural reefs by heavy visitor numbers. Once underwater, the aircraft's large internal and external surfaces could provide hard substrate for algae and other marine organisms, while openings and sheltered spaces could eventually offer refuge for fish and other aquatic species. Similar artificial reefs around the world have been created using deliberately submerged ships, concrete structures and other carefully prepared materials, although the ecological value of such projects depends heavily on factors including water quality, location, materials and the species already present in the surrounding ecosystem.How the retired passenger jet became an underwater habitatThe A300 had spent its earlier life carrying passengers through the sky, but after retirement it was given an entirely different purpose on the seabed. Its fuselage, wings and other structures created a large artificial surface in an environment where hard surfaces can become colonised by marine organisms over time. Officials hoped that this process would turn the aircraft into a functioning artificial reef while simultaneously giving recreational divers a distinctive site to explore. The project also reflected Turkey's wider interest in using artificial underwater structures to stimulate marine tourism and create additional habitat. Rather than allowing the retired aircraft to be dismantled and disappear from public view, authorities effectively repurposed it as a permanent underwater attraction. More than a decade after the sinking, the Kuşadası Airbus remains one of the world's more unusual examples of an aircraft being deliberately transformed from a piece of aviation infrastructure into an artificial marine environment.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: North Korea launched 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards its eastern waters on Thursday, a day after it dismissed US President Donald Trump’s efforts to resume diplomacy, when he ordered to scale back of military drills with South KoreaThe missiles were reportedly launched from the region of Pyongyang at around 5 pm, prompting the South Korean military to tighten its surveillance.The joint chiefs of staff said the military was closely coordinating information regarding the launches with the US and Japan. Earlier, the Japanese prime minister’s office had reported detecting a suspected missile launch.Following the launches, the national security council held an emergency meeting, then issued a statement urging North Korea to halt the launches, which are banned under UN security council resolutions, the Guardian reported.Trump’s effort to mend relations with North KoreaOn Wednesday, the South Korean and US militaries said they were scaling back their 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises by six days, and would now conclude on Friday. Seoul said the "period and scale" adjustments were made due to a "proposal of the US side".Trump had reportedly ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the exercises just before they began on Monday.Explaining his reasons for the decision, the US president cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong-un, and South Korea’s refusal to support him over the war against Iran.Kim Yo-jong, the influential sister of the North Korean leader, dismissed Trump’s overture on Wednesday, saying it was not worthy of comment.“The provocative, aggressive nature of the drills won’t change even though their duration and size were reduced,” she said. “If the US calculates that it can propagate its recent measure as one of so-called good faith, they will not get the desired answer.”She also pointed to a series of other military drills conducted by the US and South Korea earlier this year, as well as South Korea’s push to introduce nuclear-powered submarines.However, according to AP, Kim Yo-jong refrained from the typically harsh rhetoric used by North Korea, saying that relations between her brother and Trump were “still excellent”.She also referred to Kim Jong-un’s previous comments that he still had “good memories” of Trump.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: An Iowa family moved the entire $12,000  farmhouse four miles on wheels to create their dream home
articles.summary: US News: When Sha’rel Moore and her husband, Brandon, bought three acres of abandoned land in northwest Iowa in 2024, they dreamed of creating a home where the.
articles.body: When Sha’rel Moore and her husband, Brandon, bought three acres of abandoned land in northwest Iowa in 2024, they dreamed of creating a home where they could raise their growing family. The property already contained an old farmhouse, but the couple soon realised that restoring it would cost more than they could afford. Rather than abandon their plans, they found an unusual alternative, a 1920 farmhouse located just four miles away. The previous owners had built a new home and were willing to sell the century-old property for $12,000. The Moores decided to buy it and undertake the extraordinary task of moving the entire structure to their own land. Once relocated, the farmhouse became the foundation for their dream home, although extensive repairs and renovations were still needed. The family's restoration journey later attracted hundreds of thousands of followers online, turning their ambitious home transformation into a widely followed project. Moving the farmhouse allowed the couple to preserve an existing piece of local history while giving the old structure a new chapter on their family's property.Why the Iowa family moved the entire farmhouse four milesThe decision allowed the family to preserve the character of an older home without taking on the cost of rebuilding from scratch. Moore told AOL that the farmhouse appealed to the family because of its spacious rooms, high ceilings and original details, but relocating it was only the beginning of the challenge. Once renovation work began, the family discovered structural damage that had not been immediately apparent. The problems added both time and expense, illustrating the difficulties that can arise when restoring a house more than 100 years old. Despite the setbacks, the Moores continued with a largely hands-on approach. They eventually estimated that around $80,000 had been spent on repairs and renovations, considerably more than the original purchase price but still part of their effort to create a permanent family home.Why the family documented the renovation onlineMoore initially began sharing the project on social media to keep her husband's family in Washington state updated, particularly his 90-year-old grandfather. What started as a way of sharing progress with relatives soon attracted an international audience, with hundreds of thousands of people following the farmhouse's transformation. The family also wanted to show a less polished side of home renovation. Rather than presenting an expensive, professionally managed makeover, Moore documented the work, unexpected problems and do-it-yourself projects involved in bringing the property back to life. The timing made the project even more demanding. Moore was pregnant with the couple's third son during the renovation while she and Brandon were also raising their two older children. Support from viewers became an unexpected part of the journey, with followers regularly checking in on both the family and the house's progress.Preserving the farmhouse's original characterWhile modernising the property, the couple remained determined to retain its historic features. They carefully removed and stored the original woodwork, with plans to refinish and reinstall it rather than replace it with newer materials. The family also hopes to restore the historic outbuildings surrounding the house. The goal was never to follow a particular interior design trend. Instead, Moore said the family wanted the house to feel warm, comfortable and lived in while keeping costs under control. After moving in, they began shifting their attention from major construction towards landscaping, exterior work and smaller personal touches. For the Moores, relocating the farmhouse ultimately became about more than finding an affordable building. It gave a century-old structure another life while allowing their family to create the home they had originally envisioned on their own property.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1982, a California cheese maker donated thousands of acres from his dairy ranch; 44 years later crews removed his old cattle levees and reconnected the San Joaquin River to 220 acres of floodplain
articles.summary: US News: For over 70 years, a section of California’s San Joaquin River was cut off from the land it once naturally fed. Old levees, not built to hold back a r.
articles.body: For over 70 years, a section of California’s San Joaquin River was cut off from the land it once naturally fed. Old levees, not built to hold back a river but to hold cattle, had quietly changed the landscape. Then in 2026 crews started to undo that history. Great Valley Grasslands State Park, outside Merced, was the scene of a celebration on June 11, as dozens of scientists, Tribal leaders, state officials, conservationists and community members gathered to mark the completion of a restoration project that took more than 15 years to bring to fruition. The Grasslands Floodplain Restoration Project, finished in February 2026, has reconnected the San Joaquin River to over 220 acres of historic floodplain habitat. The project is returning the river to its natural overflow across the grasslands, by breaching sections of old levees. It’s a remarkable environmental turnaround — and one that began with an unlikely gift from a California dairy farmer and cheesemaker. Scroll down to understand the relation between the project and cheesemaker.A river at last finds its way homeAccording to the American Rivers website news report, the June gathering was more than a ceremonial occasion. It was the return of a natural process that had been absent from this landscape for over 75 years. After speeches by state officials, tribal representatives and conservation leaders, attendees walked along the San Joaquin River to the newly breached levee. A red ribbon was draped across the new channel. It is reported that American Rivers led the project’s implementation, in partnership with California State Parks, River Partners and Flow West. The event was one of five spotlight events highlighting conservation efforts across the state as part of California State Parks Week. “Restoration is not a sprint, nor is it a marathon. That’s a relay, a passing of the torch from one generation to the next to care for the land,” said Ann Willis, California regional director for American Rivers.Why we care about floodplainsThe report states that floodplains are much more than a coincidence of flooding. They are some of the most productive ecosystems on earth, providing habitat for plants and animals and performing important functions for people. When rivers can flow over their natural floodplains, water slows, filters through soil and helps recharge underground aquifers. The newly reconnected floodplain along the San Joaquin River is expected to provide a variety of benefits. Also, seasonal flooding can help reduce invasive plants that prefer drier conditions and improve conditions for native grasses and wetland plants. These plants also provide food and shelter for wildlife. It is also believed to benefit threatened and endangered fish species, including Chinook salmon. And, floodplain areas can offer juvenile salmon relatively sheltered waters and access to food during a critical stage of their development.A home for wildlife and vernal poolsAs per the report, seasonal flooding can also create vernal pools, temporary wetlands that form during wet periods and dry up as conditions become drier. These pools may be temporary, but are important habitats for a variety of amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates. Their lives rely on seasonal patterns of water and soil that have been disturbed in many areas of California. So, restoring those rhythms is more than just restoring water to the land. It is about restoring a connected ecosystem in which water, plants, fish and wildlife can respond to seasonal cycles once more.An improbable beginning: A dairy farmIf we go by the news report by American Rivers, Great Valley Grasslands State Park has a story with a peculiar beginning. Joseph Gallo was a former dairy farmer who built a successful cheese business. In 1982, he donated thousands of acres of Central Valley grasslands to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the state of California. He requested that the land be preserved as wildlife refuges and parks. Today, Great Valley Grasslands State Park covers nearly 2,826 acres south of Modesto and west of Merced. It includes one of the largest remaining areas of native grassland in California. When Gallo donated the property, old levees, built in the 1950s, still crossed the grasslands. They were not intended to control the San Joaquin River. Instead, they served as a means of corralling cattle within the dairy operation.A 15-year effort to reverse the pastMore than 15 years ago, American Rivers began working with California State Parks, River Partners and other agencies, nonprofit organizations and private partners to learn how to restore the park’s native grasslands and reconnect the river to its floodplain. Permitting problems and the realities of working in an area that nature designed to flood have delayed the project. Weather and flooding could halt construction for months, making work impossible. Some of the State Parks staff and engineers were involved in the project for over 15 years. Funding eventually came from a number of sources, including California Department of Fish and Wildlife funding through Propositions 1 and 68, California State Parks’ Cannabis Watershed Protection Program and support from Cox Enterprises. The result was a restoration project that can re-connect the river to over 220 acres of floodplain.The work is not done yet Construction is not the end of the project. This is the start of a new phase: what the ecosystem does Water temperatures, groundwater levels, zooplankton, native vegetation and wildlife activity will be monitored by scientists and restoration teams.The zooplankton are of special importance as they are part of the food web that supports young salmon. When water passes through the recently breached areas, populations of zooplankton on the floodplain and in the river can be compared to determine whether the restored habitat is providing the ecological benefits expected. The information gained here could also help to inform future floodplain restoration efforts along the San Joaquin River and elsewhere.A new future for the central valleyThe restoration comes as California's Central Valley looks for more ways to provide opportunities for people to experience and protect its natural landscapes. The region has historically been one of the least park-rich in the state, with many of California’s parks situated along the coast or in mountain regions. California State Parks is seeking public input for a General Plan to improve access to Great Valley Grasslands State Park. Meanwhile, State Parks and American Rivers continue to work on plans to restore and reconnect more than 1,000 additional acres north of the San Joaquin River, purchased with funding from the Wildlife Conservation Board.The state is also turning its attention to parks in the Central Valley. In April, Governor Gavin Newsom announced State Parks Forward, a program that includes plans for three new state parks in the region, including the 874-acre San Joaquin River Parkway in Fresno.Images Courtesy: istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: New York started digging Water Tunnel No. 3 in 1970; water reached all of Manhattan only in 2013, 43 years later
articles.summary: US News: Explore the 43-year-long construction journey of New York's City Water Tunnel No. 3, which finally brought water to Manhattan in 2013, enhancing the city's drinking water system and ensuring redundancy for older tunnels.
articles.body: In 1970, New York City began construction of what would eventually become one of the most ambitious infrastructure projects in its history: City Water Tunnel No. 3. The project was designed to create a third major conduit for the city’s drinking-water system and, crucially, provide enough redundancy to allow the two older tunnels to be inspected and repaired. In 1998, the first sections entered service, but the Manhattan portion was not activated till 2013, meaning the project had been under construction for 43 years. According to the New York City Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), the tunnel ultimately stretches for more than 60 miles through the city’s underground bedrock.Why New York City required a third tunnelFor the major part of the 20th century, New York City depended primarily on two water tunnels. Tunnel No. 1 entered service in 1917, and Tunnel No. 2 followed in 1936. DEP reported that both tunnels were deep beneath the city and carried water from New York’s upstate supply system toward the five boroughs. By the middle of the century, officials recognised a fundamental problem, that is, taking either tunnel out of service for major inspections or any repairs would threaten the reliability of the city’s water supply. They believed the answer to this problem was building a third tunnel that could operate alongside the older pair.While the construction for the third tunnel began in 1970, the progress was far from straightforward. The project was divided into stages and required enormous underground shafts, chambers and connections to the existing distribution network. As per a New York City planning report, the original project was estimated to cost about $1.5 billion and take 16 years. However, delays and changing requirements eventually led the cost to exceed $6 billion. In 2026, the ongoing expansion has extended construction across more than half a century. Modern DEP project data for the mid-2020s shows that this protracted development window has successfully transformed the tunnel from a singular engineering project into a continuously evolving, multi-generational utility network.Nevertheless, the first section reached completion, with Stage 1 running approximately 13 miles from Hillview Reservoir in Yonkers through the Bronx, beneath Manhattan and across the East River toward Queens. This section entered service in 1998, thus beginning the gradual expansion of Tunnel No. 3’s role in the city’s water network.Digging hundreds of feet beneath ManhattanThe Manhattan portion presented another engineering challenge. While the operational Stage 1 tunnel had already established a primary northern backbone beneath the island in 1998, securing full borough-wide backup capability required a localized distribution network. The construction on the distinct Stage 2 Manhattan delivery circuit began in 2003, and excavation took place roughly 550 feet below the city streets in some parts. DEP reported that the tunnel extended from the West Side near 30th Street toward Lower Manhattan and then northward along the eastern side of the island. Additionally, crews constructed shafts that would eventually connect the deep tunnel to the water mains closer to the surface.It is worth noting that the tunnel itself was not simply a giant pipe running directly beneath every neighbourhood. Instead, a network of shafts and distribution chambers was required to connect the deep conduit to New York’s existing water-main system. These shafts serve as conduits through which water reaches local distribution mains. In 2010, DEP announced the completion of 8.5 miles of tunnelling and concrete lining along the Manhattan region, together with 10 shafts.However, the final connection took years after the principal tunnelling was completed, as new trunk water mains had to be installed so that the water from the tunnel could actually enter the existing distribution network. In 2013, the city announced completion of around 2,750 feet of new trunk mains on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, describing the work as a crucial step toward activating the Manhattan section later that year.That distinction is important when describing the project in 2013, as the Water Tunnel No. 3 was not first completed in 2013, nor did water reach Manhattan for the first time that year. Stage 1 section had already been delivering water since it entered service in 1998. Therefore, 2013 marked the activation of the Manhattan portion of Stage 2, extending the new tunnel’s service and redundancy within the island.On 16 October 2013, Mayor Michael Bloomberg announced the completion and activation of the Manhattan section. This milestone marked the precise point where the city achieved the operational security needed to safely begin isolating its aging predecessors. While Tunnel No. 1, built in 1917, had already crossed the century mark and Tunnel No. 2, built in 1936, was rapidly approaching it, the activation of the Stage 2 loop finally removed the existential risk of a citywide water shortage. This redundancy cleared the way for authorities to safely execute the highly complex, phased shutdowns and internal automated inspections of these older conduits.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Lianna Genovese, an 19-year-old Canadian student whose gadget made from straws, sponge and pipes helps people with cerebral palsy rediscover painting; now sells in over 25 countries
articles.summary: US News: An estimated 18 million people of all ages live with cerebral palsy across the globe. Within the United States, this number ranges from 764,000 to 1 m.
articles.body: An estimated 18 million people of all ages live with cerebral palsy across the globe. Within the United States, this number ranges from 764,000 to 1 million, with about 1 in every 345 children diagnosed, according to the Cerebral Palsy Guide. Most such kids are unable to entertain themselves with the toys and activities that others their age do. But one Canadian student's invention has helped children with cerebral palsy venture into the art of painting.Straws, pipe cleaners, and sponges would seem of no use to an engineering student other than their one true purpose. But for Lianna Genovese, they sparked an idea that went beyond her room into hospitals, schools and homes in dozens of countries. The inspiration came when she met Elissa, introduced through the James Dyson Award and McMaster University as a woman with cerebral palsy who had lost the ability to use a brush and subsequently, her ability to paint as she once did. Genovese was only 18, a first-year student and studying biomedical and mechanical engineering at McMaster University in Canada. They met through a classroom project where Genovese and her classmates were working to help Elissa.The will to change livesWhile other students focused on an ergonomic computer mouse or other daily-use items, Genovese’s group members looked for a way to help the avid artist paint again. “I wanted to give Elissa back her passion,” recalled Genovese. Upon learning of Elissa's story, she began thinking of ways to leverage the movements that the woman was still able to perform to guide a brush across a surface. In a statement made by the university in 2021, Genovese explained that hearing about the story ignited her desire to restore part of Elissa's capacity for expression.This is when she formed a principle that formed the base of the final project: using larger movements of the arm and shoulder to compensate for the limitations of fine hand movements. According to the James Dyson Award and McMaster University, the first prototypes were assembled with straws, pipe cleaners, and a sponge. She collaborated with Elissa who participated in testing and provided feedback on what she could or could not do with the equipment.Based on these experiences, new versions began to emerge. The project continued to be refined with the involvement of individuals with differing medical conditions, along with neurologists and occupational therapists. By 2021, Lianna had already spoken to or tested with more than 150 patients and healthcare professionals in Canada, according to McMaster University.Two years later, the university reported that the development had already received contributions from more than 525 occupational therapists, neurologists, and individuals with limited hand mobility.3D printer-inspired system that guides hand movementsThe most advanced version of Guided Hands adopted a logic reminiscent of the movement of a 3D printer. The device has a structure made up of linear axes and bearings that allows for guided hand movement. With this, the user can perform horizontal and vertical movements and also change the direction of the motion. The person rests their hand on an adapted piece and moves the whole setup mainly using the larger motor skills of the shoulder and arm. Different objects can be attached at the end, such as a pen, marker, brush, or a stylus for touch screens.It does not paint or write on its own and rather functions as a structure that supports and guides the movement performed by the individual themselves. This ensures that the user's participation is vital.Beyond an experimentAmong the tests conducted during the development, one meeting changed Genovese's thoughts on the device. She met Bella, a girl with cerebral palsy and observed her using Guided Hands to write, colour, draw and play on an iPad. According to the engineer, watching the girl’s reaction made her realise that this college project could have much broader applications beyond the classroom.The experience helped transform an academic activity into a venture. She founded ImaginAble Solutions in 2019, while she was still a third-year student, to develop and commercialise assistive technologies. In an initial phase, the very structure used to develop the product operated in the basement of the young entrepreneur’s home, according to a report published by McMaster.In August 2021, Genovese won the Canadian stage of the James Dyson Award, an international design and engineering competition aimed at students and recent graduates. She secured the national prize of US$3,500 to further develop the invention and also qualified the device for the international phase of the competition.At that time, the expectation was to bring the equipment to market by the end of 2021. However, commercial development continued through testing and programs with hospitals and rehabilitation centres. McMaster later reported that the product officially entered the market when Lianna graduated in 2022.What started as inexpensive materials assembled to test a movement is now being manufactured in the Hamilton region of Ontario and distributed internationally.Moreover, in 2023, Genovese was also included in the Forbes 30 Under 30 Local Toronto list. In 2024, she received the Muhammad Ali Humanitarian Award for her work on inclusion and quality of life for people with disabilities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, Belgium raised semi-transparent solar panels above a working pear orchard; pear yields fell 15%, but combined land-use efficiency reached 44% higher
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Belgium's innovative agrivoltaics project raised semi-transparent solar panels over a pear orchard, revealing a 15% drop in pear yield but a remarkable 44% increase in land productivity through dual food and electricity generation.
articles.body: In 2020, researchers in Belgium installed a row of semi-transparent solar panels above a working pear orchard in Bierbeek, near Leuven. The experiment was designed to test whether the same land could produce both food and electricity without sacrificing too much of either. Three years of harvest data now offer a clearer picture of the trade-off. Pear production fell by about 15% under the panels, but the combined use of the land achieved a land-equivalent ratio of 1.44, indicating that the agrivoltaic system made more productive use of the land than separate food and electricity production.According to KU Leuven, researchers began monitoring the orchard during the 2021 growing season to examine how the panels affected pear trees and fruit. The Bierbeek project was conducted under commercial orchard conditions, allowing researchers to assess how agrivoltaics performed in an active agricultural setting. The trial also examined whether the panels could provide additional benefits for the orchard while generating renewable electricity. Researchers also compared conditions beneath the panels with those in uncovered parts of the orchard, tracking factors such as tree growth, fruit development and microclimate. The results helped show how solar infrastructure could be integrated into an existing orchard without removing the agricultural use of the land.A solar roof over the pearsThe installation was designed specifically for the trees. Conventional solar panels would have blocked too much sunlight, so researchers selected semi-transparent photovoltaic modules that allowed part of the incoming light to reach the pear canopy. The panels were mounted about 4.2 metres above the ground, directly over rows of Conference pear trees, and covered roughly a quarter of the ground area with photovoltaic modules.The arrangement was not intended merely to generate electricity. The panels were attached to the orchard's existing hail-protection structure, allowing the researchers to test whether the solar installation could provide agricultural benefits alongside its energy output. The panels also altered the orchard's microclimate. KU Leuven's research found that the system increased nighttime air temperatures during periods of frost by about 0.5°C and reduced the peaks of high temperatures during a hot summer period. The structure could also provide physical protection against hail and reduce exposure to intense sunlight, potentially helping to limit weather-related damage to the crop.But the experiment also revealed a clear trade-off. Pear trees need sufficient sunlight for photosynthesis and fruit development, and the panels reduced the amount of light reaching the canopy. During the three-year assessment, researchers recorded an average reduction in light of about 24%. The key question was whether this reduction would lead to a comparable decline in pear production.Less fruit, but more from the same landThe answer was consistent across three growing seasons. According to Agronomy for Sustainable Development, pears grown under the agrivoltaic system produced about 15% less fruit than those in the control plots in each of the three years. Yields fell from 42.6 to 35.7 tonnes per hectare in 2021, from 52.6 to 44.7 tonnes per hectare in 2022 and from 47.6 to 41.1 tonnes per hectare in 2023. The reduction did not mean the pears were generally lower in quality. Flowering and fruit set did not change significantly, while most measured quality characteristics remained similar between the shaded and unshaded fruit. However, researchers did observe more bottle-shaped pears and a reduction in fruit calibre under the panels.That distinction matters because agrivoltaics is judged by more than crop yield. Its central argument is that electricity and food can be produced from the same piece of land. The researchers therefore calculated a land-equivalent ratio, which compares combined production with what would be achieved if the agricultural and solar activities occupied separate areas. The three-year experiment reached an average ratio of 1.44. In practical terms, the combined system was using land 44% more efficiently than separate production of pears and electricity under the study's calculation.A model with limitsThe Bierbeek experiment ultimately suggests that agrivoltaics works best when it is designed around the needs of a particular crop rather than applied as a universal solution. The orchard did not produce the same harvest under the panels, but the land was able to provide two outputs at once: fruit and electricity. That makes the system less about replacing conventional farming and more about finding ways to use agricultural land more efficiently.The results also point to a broader question for future projects. Agrivoltaics will have to prove that its benefits can outweigh the compromises involved, not only in terms of crop production but also through reliable electricity generation and long-term economic returns. Further research will therefore be important to determine whether systems tested in orchards such as Bierbeek can become practical at a larger scale.For farmers, the appeal of such systems may ultimately depend on whether the additional electricity revenue can compensate for any reduction in agricultural output. The Bierbeek project therefore provides a useful real-world test of that trade-off. Rather than showing that solar panels and farming always work better together, it demonstrates the need to assess both sides of the equation before converting productive farmland to an agrivoltaic system.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
